title.analysis: Authentic title "The Psychology of Money Nobody Talks About (Money Anxiety Explained)" promises an explanatory, under-discussed angle. The script delivers a general essay on financial anxiety, money scripts, inherited trauma, environment-based discipline, present bias and future-self thinking; "nobody talks about" is overstated (Housel's book and the money-scripts literature are mainstream), and the title borrows the well-known book name.

script.opening_words: Have you ever felt your heart race when opening a credit card statement? Maybe you've avoided checking your bank account for weeks because the anxiety feels overwhelming. Or perhaps you find yourself making completely irrational financial decisions that you can't explain even to yourself. If any of this sounds familiar, you're definitely not alone and more importantly, you're not broken. What you're experiencing has a name and understanding it might just change everything about how you handle money. My name
script.ending_words: someone who has choices, even when those choices are difficult. And honestly, that shift from helplessness to agency might be worth more than any investment return you'll ever see. Uh if this video helped you understand why you do what you do with money, hit that like button, and let me know in the comments what money script you recognize in yourself, because I guarantee you're not the only one.
script.analysis: Full 21283 canonical characters read. A single-narrator essay without composites or worked numbers: hook on money anxiety, Experian 68% trauma statistic, foundation metaphor, anxiety symptoms and the Payoff PTSD figures, generational trauma, money scripts, falling self-reported discipline, environment design (automation, cash, removing apps), loss vs gain framing, 48-hour rule, present bias, gamification, financial therapy, future-self visualisation, and a close on agency. Only three statistics are quoted; two are older surveys presented as current and one is clinically overstated.

claim_audit.assessment: Verified as a reported survey result: Experian's October 2023 survey of about 2,000 US adults found 68% believe they have suffered or are suffering financial trauma. Self-reported perception, not a clinical measure; the script's 'recent' is two years before publication.

claim_audit.assessment: Misstated: the figures trace to Payoff's 2016 online survey (about 2,000 respondents; 23% overall, about 35-36% of millennials) describing PTSD-like symptoms it labelled Acute Financial Stress. It was a symptom-overlap screen by a fintech company, not a clinical diagnosis, and is nine years old at publication.
